en: I have lived long and seen many days.
My son's only child, Semetey—
I kept wondering whether he would come.
Tearing my heart apart,
They raised him far away,
My one boy Semetey.
When Semetey comes to mind,
My heart burns, my liver is a live coal.
My darling camel-calf left by Manas,
Bakai, I have no sorrow but my child.
I go on living for that soul.
The reason I pass my days in lamentation
Is that one boy Semetey.
Ah, prophet-like warrior Bakai,
If my orphan has come,
I shall agree to what you say,
That treasure, those many gold coins,
All of them, Khan Bakai,
I shall give as a reward for good news.
Do not think my intentions are otherwise.
Bring before my eyes,
Let me see for myself,
My one boy Semetey.
That jewel upon my brow,
Bring him to me.
Semetey, the mirror set upon my brow,
Bakai, let my eyes see him.
If you bring him to me,
I shall agree to what you say.
All the livestock without a master
I shall give as a reward for good news.
Take my imposing swift steeds.
As your reward, kill me and take my life!
Alas, Bakai, heed my words.
I shall give it as a reward:
Take my red-tailed elephant outside!
Leave two of mine and take one;
Leave my file and take my whetstone;
Leave my old wife and take my people!
Gold and treasure,
I shall give you without begrudging them.
My lion Bakai, take them yourself!
My orphan left by my warrior son Manas,
Will he not grow weary with longing?
Will the sun's heat not strike him?
My only one, found late in life,
Will he not shiver in the cold?
Will God not take him thus?
My cherished only one,
Will he not fall ill?”
When Zhakyp said this,
Warrior Bakai listened carefully.
Wearing a cap of gray lynx fur,
Wolf-maned Bakai the Leopard,
Your champion who had seen much,
Your clairvoyant saint Bakai,
Heard Zhakyp's words again.
Then old Bakai,
Unable to tell friend from foe,
Khan Bakai, bewildered,
Mounted Kokcholok.
Wolf-maned Bakai set off.
No wind could match his trot.
That day, Kokcholok—
No horse could match his walk.
When Kokcholok merely walked,
The tips of the grass rustled.
Too swift for the eye to catch,
Bakai the Leopard moved.
Where he passed,
All the stones crumbled.
When the blessed one moved on,
The grass tips shook.
Bakai the Leopard rode on;
Allah's sun clouded in the sky.
Sixty thoughts came to him at once:
“The utterly kinless orphan
I must not bring straight here.
That khan was like a swine.
Without first probing his secret,
I must not hand over my orphan.
The grandfather, the swine khan,
Was a man of evil intent.
His conduct and his heart
Were like an infidel's.
He had little care for his people.
Not only toward the son—this swine
Toward my Manas himself
Bore enmity.
He used to grumble and burn with anger:
‘The myriad livestock brought from Altai,
Manas drove away and lost,
And thus made a fool of me,’ he said.
That was what he used to say.
If Zhakyp is honest,
Let me see his pure heart.
If Zhakyp is wicked,
Let me learn the fool's secret.”
So saying, Khan Bakai,
That exceedingly powerful saint,
Whether he was wicked or honest,
That fatherly elder Zhakyp,
The old man now meant to test.
He raced away,
Then raced back again.
He turned Kokcholok's head.
Prince Bakai the Leopard,
At the side wall of Khan Zhakyp's dwelling,
Stood listening to his words.
Khan Zhakyp lay crying aloud,
Weeping and wailing then:
“Old woman, do you know what I know?
Do you sense what I sense?
The pit dug ready has arrived;
The mighty trouble brewing has arrived.
A fire to burn us has arrived;
A day of misfortune, a great ordeal, has come for my sons.
Old woman, the more it is spent, the more it blazes—
“The heir of that mighty champion
The more it dies, the more it increases—
The offspring of that one who should burn!
He who poured blood into clear water,
The very son of calamity,
He who burned the grassy land—
The only child of that one who should burn
Will bring us no good in the end.
Old woman, he will not leave my sons unharmed!
My countless cattle earned through toil,
My myriad livestock earned from grain,
All of it was destroyed
Own son of turbulent Manas,
If we do not slaughter this orphan,
He will bring my offspring no good.
He will not let the plow turn,
Will not let my six sons dwell in this Talas.
Let us work a wonder upon the orphan;
Let us wipe out this wretch like putting out a fire.
Before he reaches maturity,
Let us kill him without delay,
And thus bring about his death.
Uprooting a green onion,
Let us treat him as though pulling it out.
A young sapling,
Let us treat him as though cutting it down.
All who hear of it,
Let us make them quail.
Cutting the poplar at its root,
Old woman, let us clear it away.
Unless we do this, he will bring us no good,
Will not leave my sons unharmed.
Take my red-tailed elephant;
My precious old woman, heed my words!
Mix honey for Khan Bakai.
Let us put it out like a fire;
Mix poison for Semetey!”
The senior wife Baidoolot,
When Khan Zhakyp spoke thus,
Leaped up, the blessed woman.
“You wretched old baldhead, you will never change!
Always raving foolishly,
You never give up your mischief.
Always, of wicked schemes,
You think of sixty.
One of seven days is death;
Sooner or later you will die.
Giving poison to your own child,
If what is said is true,
When the dawn of Judgment comes,
What answer will you give?
Against that tender gray-mottled falcon,
How could you raise your hand,
Against that gray goshawk, that morning star?
He is the pennant fixed upon your spear,
The gift left by magnanimous Manas.
To the hoof left by the swift steed,
How can you give poison,
To that dear, unbred noble steed?
If you do this, baldhead, you will not prosper.
If you kill your own child,
You will never prosper.
It is a terrible thing to consume a shroud.
Could anyone be as shroudless as you?
The dear child granted by fate—
Alas, can one who means to kill him prosper?
Can there be a Muslim like you?
Could one who calls an infidel like you
A Muslim ever prosper?
To an infidel like you,
Would any person listen?
With what face could you give it
To the child born of your khan Manas?
You prepare poison for your own child;
Could he have an heir like you?
Could anyone calling you a Muslim prosper?
Well, can there be a Muslim like you?
Without a post to tether a horse,
Such utter bareness is yours.
Giving poison to your own child,
Such infidelity is yours!
Can there be a Muslim like you?
Could anyone who calls you righteous prosper?
Through your hot temper, old man,
You became known as the swine khan.
Can there be a human like you?
Manas's only son Semetey,
That dear child found late in life—
How can you set upon him?
May this deed of yours come to nothing!
Let your six sons gather together,
And all be sacrificed for Manas alone!
When Manas lived,
I studied the words of the Haftiyak,
And rinsed my mouth with rich fat.
Poor soul who would not draw the roof-cover,
When my only one, Manas, passed away,
This hair of mine turned white.
When Manas the Leopard lived,
I was one who sliced belly fat.
Since Manas the Leopard passed away,
I have been despised worse than a Kalmyk.
When valiant Manas lived,
My wondrous treasury,
All my kinds of livestock were in readiness.
Over the eighteen thousand worlds
I used to stand as khan.
At the entrance to my door,
My tigers bred fifteen times.
No one dared approach.
There were sixty dragons,
And on this side of them
Stood elephants with sword-like trunks.
When Manas, blessed by Kydyr, lived,
Who else lived like this?
Since that Manas passed away,
Since he went to the next world,
Before your doorway
There is not a puppy, let alone a tiger.
For that son Manas,
Your children, the six wicked ones at their head,
Let them all be sacrificed!
When Manas lived,
We made merry in delight.
From all the different peoples,
Six thousand foals of barren mares apiece
We used to take as tribute.
Since that Manas passed away,
There is not a green ear of corn, let alone tribute.
Children worth less than a green ear,
Those half-made six wicked ones—
Can they be called children?
A wolf-maned man like Manas—
Can one who speaks of him like this prosper?
Was plundered by the six scoundrels;
Can these be called children?
When my Manas lived,
Not a millet grain would fit in this mouth.
